title: XDMA and PCIe
excerpt: What is BAR? BAR => Base Address Register It is a small register located on the PCIe card During boot:   BIOS walks PCIe bus and finds every card  For each card it reads how many BARs the card h...
content: What is BAR? BAR => Base Address Register It is a small register located on the PCIe card During boot:   BIOS walks PCIe bus and finds every card  For each card it reads how many BARs the card has and how big each BAR wants to be  BIOS finds free space in the CPU’s physicall address map and writes starting address into each BAR  When CPU accesses an address in that range the chipset routes it to that card  Host sees physical address while the card sees offsets from within its own BARWhat is XDMA? XDMA is a Xilinx IP which handles the PCIe protocol It exposes 3 BARs which connects to different AXI master interfaces   DMA BAR => Drives M_AXI  AXI-lite BAR => Drives M_AXI_LITE  Bypass BAR => Drives M_AXI_Bypass  Host writes to BAR Addr + Offset and FPGA M_AXI will see Offset In Linux the driver provides a file /dev/xdma0_h2c_0 where the file offset = AXI Address so writing to that file is like doing a memory write to that address For AXI-Lite that file is /dev/xdma0_user, as for AXI-Lite there is another parameter which is translation offset   Translation offset allows you shift where the BAR window sits for example if your translation offset is 0x40000000 then with host offset 0x100 the FPGA will write to 0x40000100  This allows small BARs to be able to reach slaves that have high FPGA addresses without wasting host address space

title: Project Overview
excerpt: Project Overview: Cross-Device Behavioral Malware Detection in IoTThe ProblemExisting syscall-based malware detectors for IoT devices achieve high accuracy (92-99%) but are trained and tested on th...
content: Project Overview: Cross-Device Behavioral Malware Detection in IoTThe ProblemExisting syscall-based malware detectors for IoT devices achieve high accuracy (92-99%) but are trained and tested on the same device type. A detector trained on a router’s syscall patterns may not work on an IP camera because their normal behaviors are fundamentally different. No existing work has tested whether these detectors actually generalize across different IoT device types.Research Questions Which behavioral signals are most effective for detecting IoT malware across multiple device types? Are there representations of the signals that generalize better across different IoT device types?ApproachEmulate multiple IoT device types using FirmAE and collect multiple behavioral signals from each under benign and malware-infected conditions. Compare different feature representations to see which generalizes best across devices.Feature Representations Raw syscall n-grams (baseline, from Sequencegram) Syscall frequency vectors Semantic category n-grams (manually grouping syscalls by function like NETWORK, FILE_IO, PROCESS) Learned embeddings via word2vec (data-driven grouping)Training Conditions Same-device: train and test on the same device type (baseline) Cross-device: train on one device type, test on another Pooled: train on all device types combined, test on eachDevices Targeting 5 device types:   Router  IP Camera  Access Point  NAS  Smart home hub / print server / media device  Aiming for multiple firmwares for each device type so that we could also cover maybe different architectures

title: Domain Adversial Training of Neural Networks
excerpt: Domain Adversial Training of Neural NetworksNotes are made from the paper: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1505.07818 Domain Adaptation - Learning a discriminative classifer in the presence of a shi...
content: Domain Adversial Training of Neural NetworksNotes are made from the paper: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1505.07818 Domain Adaptation - Learning a discriminative classifer in the presence of a shit between training and test distributions   Like training a semtiment analyser on movie reviews but testing on books reviews since there isn’t enough training data for book reviews   The paper proposes building mappings between source and target distributions  “Good representation for cross-domain transfer is one for which an algorithim cannot learn to identify the domain of origin of input” H-Divergence: Measure of the distance between two distributions based on how specific class of classifers can tell them apart   The bigger the H-Divergence the bigger the difference between distributions  Target Risk Bound: Error rate in target domain is limited by 3 things   Error in source  H-Divergence  Constant term representing best possible error shared by both domains.   Proxy A-distance (PAD) - Used as approximate since H-Divergence is hard to calculate Effective domain transfer requires domain-invariant features which are internal representations of data that are:   Discriminative - Contain enough information to correctly predict labels  Indiscriminate - Do not contain enough information that would allow system to distinguish where data came from  DANN system consists of:   Feature Extractor, Label predictor, Domain Classifier  Feature Extractor tries to minimize the error in the label predictor while maximizing the error in domain classifier  Gradient Reversal Layer   During forward propagation the input is left unchanged  But in back propagation the gradient is reversed by multiplying with a negative scalar     Done so that it trains adverse to domain classifier

title: Adding a New Language Keyboard to KOReader
excerpt: Adding a New Language Keyboard to KOReaderA guide for adding native keyboard layouts to KOReader (tested on 2026.03 / Kobo Clara), based on adding an Azerbaijani layout. Use this as a template for ...
content: Adding a New Language Keyboard to KOReaderA guide for adding native keyboard layouts to KOReader (tested on 2026.03 / Kobo Clara), based on adding an Azerbaijani layout. Use this as a template for any future language.Why you’d do thisKOReader ships with keyboards for many languages, but not all of them. If you’re reading books/PDFs in a language without a native layout, you either: fall back to a keyboard that’s close but wrong (e.g. using Turkish for Azerbaijani), or can’t type the language’s special characters into dictionary lookups, search, notes, etc.The fix: add a proper layout as a small patch file, not a full rewrite.The key insightDon’t write a keyboard from scratch. Every non-English KOReader layout (see tr_keyboard.lua, etc.) is built by: Loading en_keyboard.lua as a base Rearranging/inserting keys on top of it Returning the modified tableThis means you inherit, for free: Shift / Symbol layers Long-press popups (accents, alternate characters) Key widths, spacing Globe key, Enter, spacebar, backspaceYou only need to define what’s different about your language.Files involved   Purpose  Path     Keyboard layouts  .adds/koreader/frontend/ui/data/keyboardlayouts/    English base layout (reference)  .../keyboardlayouts/en_keyboard.lua    Popup/long-press definitions  .../keyboardlayouts/keypopup/en_popup.lua    Keyboard registration  .adds/koreader/frontend/ui/widget/virtualkeyboard.lua    Language name registration  .adds/koreader/frontend/ui/language.lua  Find them on your device with:find /Volumes/KOBOeReader/.adds/koreader/frontend/ui/data/keyboardlayouts -maxdepth 1 -iname "*.lua"Step-by-step1. Understand the English base layout’s structureen_keyboard.lua returns a table like:return { min_layer = 1, max_layer = 4, shiftmode_keys = { ... }, symbolmode_keys = { ... }, utf8mode_keys = { ... }, keys = {  -- Row 1: number row  -- Row 2: Q W E R T Y U I O P (10 keys)  -- Row 3: A S D F G H J K L , (10 keys, last is punctuation)  -- Row 4: [Shift] Z X C V B N M [Backspace] (9 keys)  -- Row 5: [Sym] [Globe] . [Space] ← → [Enter] },}Each key is a table of up to 4 entries corresponding to the 4 layers:{ Regular, Shift, Symbol, Shift+Symbol }A key can also have popup directions (long-press/swipe) as named fields:{ "Ü", north = "ü" }north/south/east/west/northeast/... map to swipe directions on that key for accented or alternate variants.2. Plan your visible layoutSketch it out first, letter by letter, e.g.:Q W E R T Y U I O P ÜA S D F G H J K L I ƏZ X C V B N M Ç Ş ÖDecide: Which English letters are simply replaced/reused as-is Which new letters need brand-new keys, and where they go Which letters pair naturally as Regular/Shift (e.g. ç/Ç) vs need their own key entirely3. Write the patch fileCreate xx_keyboard.lua (use the language’s ISO 639-1 code) in the keyboardlayouts/ folder:local xx_keyboard = dofile("frontend/ui/data/keyboardlayouts/en_keyboard.lua")local keys = xx_keyboard.keys-- Insert a new key into a row at a specific position.-- table.insert automatically shifts everything after it right,-- so existing keys (e.g. the comma key) move over safely.table.insert(keys[3], 10, { { "Ə", north = "ə", }, { "ə", north = "Ə", }, "Ə", "ə", })-- Replace an existing key entirely (e.g. swap English "I" for-- a language-specific dotless/dotted pair):keys[2][8][1] = { "I", north = "ı" }keys[2][8][2] = { "ı", north = "I" }-- Optional: translate the spacebar labelkeys[5][4].label = "boşluq"return xx_keyboardTips: Always table.insert rather than overwrite when adding new keys, so you don’t clobber existing punctuation keys — they’ll just get pushed further along the row. Reuse north = (and south/east/west/etc.) for the uppercase/lowercase counterpart or an accented variant, matching how the rest of KOReader handles long-press. If a language has a distinctive currency symbol, it’s a nice (optional) touch to add it to the number row, the way tr_keyboard.lua adds ₺.4. Register the language nameIn frontend/ui/language.lua, find language_names = { and add:xx = "Native Language Name",5. Register the keyboard layoutIn frontend/ui/widget/virtualkeyboard.lua, find lang_to_keyboard_layout = { and add:xx = "xx_keyboard",6. Test on-deviceCopy xx_keyboard.lua to:.adds/koreader/frontend/ui/data/keyboardlayouts/Restart KOReader, switch to the new language via the keyboard’s globe/language switcher, and check: All new letters appear where expected Shift produces correct uppercase Long-press/swipe popups work Nothing from the original English layout (punctuation, numbers, Enter, etc.) got lost or overlapped7. (Optional) Validate the Lua syntax before copying to deviceIf you have Lua installed locally (or in a sandbox), you can sanity-check the file loads without errors before putting it on the Kobo:lua5.3 -e 'local ok, kb = pcall(dofile, "path/to/keyboardlayouts/xx_keyboard.lua")if not ok then print("LOAD ERROR:", kb) else print("Loaded OK, rows:", #kb.keys) end'This needs local copies of en_keyboard.lua and keypopup/en_popup.lua in the same relative folder structure, since xx_keyboard.lua dofiles them by relative path.Reference: rows in en_keyboard.lua   Row index  Contents  Key count     keys[1]  Numbers  10    keys[2]  Q W E R T Y U I O P  10    keys[3]  A S D F G H J K L ,  10    keys[4]  Shift, Z X C V B N M, Backspace  9    keys[5]  Sym, Globe, period, Space, ←, →, Enter  7  Worked example: AzerbaijaniSee az_keyboard.lua — adds Ü, Ə, ı, Ç, Ş, Ö on top of the English base, inserting new keys into rows 2–4 rather than rewriting them, following exactly the pattern above.

title: Notes on how to review a paper
excerpt: Notes taken from Onur Mutlu lecture on how to do paper reviews: link1. Brief Summary What is the problem paper is trying to solve? What are the key insights? What is the key contribution? What is t...
content: Notes taken from Onur Mutlu lecture on how to do paper reviews: link1. Brief Summary What is the problem paper is trying to solve? What are the key insights? What is the key contribution? What is the most important takeaways?2. Strengths Order them from the strongest to weakest strengths Does the paper solve the problem well?3. Weaknesses Again we should order them from biggest weakness to the smallest Should think critically on where there is room for improvement4. Can you do better? Present thoughts/ideas5. What have you learnt/enjoyed/disliked and why?Advice Be critical Always think of better ways to solve the problem Do background reading

title: ZUC
excerpt: Introduction  ZUC => Stream cipher used to encrypt communications in mobile networks Stream cipher   Initial seed is provided which generates a stream of data that is pseudoranom  Stream is mixe...
content: Introduction  ZUC => Stream cipher used to encrypt communications in mobile networks Stream cipher   Initial seed is provided which generates a stream of data that is pseudoranom  Stream is mixed with plain text for encryption  Receiver will have same secret key (seed), thus can generate the same keystream  Symmetric key cryptosystem   If key K is used for encrypting a message then the same key K has to be used for decryption  Divided into 2 categories: 1) Block cipher : Message is divided into multiple fixed length blocks which are then individualy encrypted with secret key, then decryption is also done block wise. 2) Stream cipher : Encryption/Decryption is done characterwise, pseudorandom sequence generated with equal length to the message, it is then bitwise XORed withe the message and the result is transmitted  One time Pad : A long sequence of pseudorandom bits where a portion of it can be used each time for encryption/decryption, but needs to be shared with reciever in advance     The distribution of One Time Pads is the issue though     Thus there is a need for a pseudorandom bit generator that also given the initial sequence of generated bits it should not be possible to efficiently guess the next bit with chances of success significantly greater than half  Prerequisites Finite Fields   A field is a nonempty set that has 2 operations, + and ·  It must also satisfy the follwing:     (F,+) is commutative   If 0 denotes is the identify element in (F,+) then (F\{0},·) is commutative   For all a,b,c ∈ F, a · (b + c) = a · b + a · c     If a field has finite elements then it is a Finite Field  If the complete multiplicative group (F\{0},·) can be generated by an element of F\{0} then (F\{0},·) is known as a cyclic group and the element is called a primative element of F\{0}  Prime fields, also called Galois Field, are fields that are the remainders of a prime p  Two Properties hold for fields:     Two finite fields with the same number of elements are isomorphic   Every finite field has exactly pⁿ elements for some prime number p and positive integer n      Field Extension   If F₂ ⊆ F₁, F₂ is closed under both operations, and F₂ is itself a field, then F₂ is a subfield of F₁, and F₁ is a field extension of F₂  Polynomials over a field   To build extensions we need to use polynomials  A polynomial over GF(p):     f(x) = c0 + c1x + c2x2+…+cmxm where ci ∈ GF(p) and cm != 0   Degree of f is m (highest power with a nonzero coefficient)     F[x] denotes the set of all polynomials with coefficients from F, but F[x] is a ring not a field  Irreducible poylnomial : Polynomial p(x) with degree ≥ 1 ∈ F[x] is irreducible if it can’t be written as p1(x) · p2(x) where both degree ≥ 1     I = ⟨p(x)⟩ = {p(x)·q(x) : q(x) ∈ F[x]}   F[x]/⟨p(x)⟩ is a field     Let p(x) be irreducible with formal root α. If α is a primitive element of the extension field (its powers generate all of F*), then p(x) is called a primitive polynomial.     Every primitive polynomial is irreducible, but not every irreducible polynomial is primitive.     Design Specification of ZUC Stream Cipher ZUC has two phases:   Key-IV initialization phase     State of the cipher will be initialized by n 128-bit secret key and a 128-bit initialization vector   Also the Key Scheduling Algorithm will run for 32 rounds without generating an output     Key Generation phase     Cipher outputs 32 bits in every round      ZUC designed based on three major components:   One Linear Feedback Shift Register  One Bit Reorganization Layer  One nonlinear function  LFSR   Usually most stream ciphers are built on extensions of GF(2) which means the LFSR will bits, but ZUC insteads is built on GF(231-1) so the LFSR holds integers     GF(231-1) is a prime field since 231-1 is a prime   The elements of the field are {1,2,…,231-1} with 0 being represented as 231-1     The LFSR is a 16 word register which each state being 31 bits     In most stream ciphers the LFSR states would be 1 bit each     ZUC uses a primitive polynomial since that guarantees maximum period. One such polynomial is:     f(x) = x¹⁶ − (2¹⁵x¹⁵ + 2¹⁷x¹³ + 2²¹x¹⁰ + 2²⁰x⁴ + (2⁸+1))   So its feedback function would be:       s₁₅t+1 = 2¹⁵s₁₅ + 2¹⁷s₁₃ + 2²¹s₁₀ + 2²⁰s₄ + (2⁸+1)s₀ (mod 2³¹−1)        Thus the state update function would be:       sit+1 = si+1t for i <= 14    s15 = 2¹⁵s₁₅ + 2¹⁷s₁₃ + 2²¹s₁₀ + 2²⁰s₄ + (2⁸+1)s₀ (mod 2³¹−1)           The addition is done using a 31 bit adder and the multiplication is done through shifting  In most cases shifting would cause overflow issues however having mod 231-1 fixes this issue:     Multiplying by 2k would just be a shift of k however if we are shifting position i (its current weight would be 2i) then its new position would be i+k   But if i+k is an overflow position then it can also be written as i+k=31+j, and the weight would be 231+j which can be split 231+j=231·2j   But since 231 is equal to 1 in mod 231-1 thus 231+j=231·2j = 1·2j   So that means the bits new position will be j which isn’t causing an overflow     The LFSR runs in two modes:     First key initialization in which the output from the nonlinear function is fed back into the LFSR and added onto the feedback (XORed in ZUC 1.4)       This is done so that similar keys don’t produce similar keystreams        Once the previous mode is done it switches to key generation where the nonlinear function is the output and not fed into the LFSR anymore      Bit Reorganization Layer   Bit Reorganization Layer consists of 4 32 bits registers, X0,X1,X2,X3  They are formed through concatentating states of the LFSR                    X0 = S15H           S14L                               X1 = S11L           S9H                               X2 = S7L           S5H                               X3 = S2L           S0H                   Nonlinear Function   Consists of 3 main componenets:     2 32-bit registers, R1 and R2   2 linear transformation functions, L1 and L2   2 S-boxes, S1 and S2 : {0,1}8 -&...
